title: The Travelling Stock Routes and Reserves of New South Wales

paragraphs.text: Routes for moving livestock such as cattle and sheep have a long history in the Australian state of New South Wales Travelling stock routes are roads along which livestock can legally be moved from one location to another. They usually have wide grass verges on either side of the road on which the animals can graze as they move along. Travelling stock reserves are fenced areas on the stock routes used for watering animals or camping overnight. Travelling stock routes and travelling stock reserves (collectively called TSRs) form a network across New South Wales (NSW). Although the main purpose of the TSR network was originally for moving large numbers of stock across the countryside, the TSR network is now recognised for its environmental, cultural and social importance. Since the advent of modern transport methods, the TSR network is no longer as widely used as it was in the past. Nonetheless, TSRs can still be an important source of feed for livestock during periods of drought, and they also provide a resource for beekeepers, who can obtain licences to place beehives on them.

The system of TSRs began early in the European settlement of Australia. The initial development of TSRs began with the spread of people moving throughout the country to set up farms. New lands were being settled and the farmers needed to move livestock to their new farms. The farmers of New South Wales pioneered the development and use of travelling stock routes. However, there is clear evidence that before Europeans arrived in Australia, the country was already crisscrossed by networks of trails that were made by the Aboriginal people, the original inhabitants of Australia, as they moved about the land. These trails connected food and water sources, and were used for travel and trade purposes. It is now thought that, in many cases, travelling stock routes developed from Aboriginal trails. This is because the trails made by the Aboriginal people often followed the most accessible ways through the landscape, avoiding natural obstacles and linking water sources. Traditional Aboriginal camping places were also sometimes used as travelling stock reserves, as is shown by the presence of artefacts such as polished stone tools and carvings on trees. As TSRs have remained open to the public, they continue to provide sites for camping and other resources to many Aboriginal communities.

As the numbers of sheep and cattle increased, the incidence of diseases also increased. Between the 1830s and the 1870s, legislation was implemented by the government in an attempt to control the spread of diseases. These controls influenced the management of TSRs in a number of ways. Most particularly, in 1864, NSW established districts that were managed and administered by a board whose members were selected from wealthy farmers living in the area covered by a district. The purpose of these districts was to inspect for and manage scab, a disease afflicting sheep that was caused by a parasitic mite. This scheme was financed by taxes that were imposed on the farmers who owned livestock in each district. Over time the districts took on more duties, and eventually began administering the TSRs. These districts underwent several name changes and eventually became the Livestock Health and Pest Authorities.

By the 1860s, travelling stock routes were used extensively by many livestock owners, so much so that some regulations were implemented to protect the rights of farmers who lived near the stock routes. Laws were brought in stipulating that animals travelling on a stock route were not to wander more than half a mile on either side of a route even if the adjacent land was unfenced. A certain speed of movement by the animals of a minimum of four miles a day was also introduced in order to protect the grazing on the routes for the animals of other users. Travelling stock reserves were established in the 1870s as camping places, and charges were also introduced for travelling stock along the routes. The pressure of the increased use on the stock routes at this time is reflected in the rise in the minimum daily travel to six miles for sheep and to ten miles for cattle.

While today TSRs in NSW are not used as much as they were in the past for moving livestock, their importance for environmental conservation remains. The TSRs act as corridors connecting patches of native vegetation. They allow native animals to travel between vegetation areas, promoting interbreeding between populations and enabling species to locate new habitats to colonise. The TSR network in NSW extends across climate zones. Temperatures in eastern Australia generally increase from south to north, whilst moisture increases from west to east. These conditions have a major influence on habitat. As the TSR network covers these climate zones, native animal species are able to move in response to changes in rainfall and temperature, particularly in response to extreme seasonal conditions such as drought. Perhaps more crucially, the network may also help animal species native to Australia to survive climate change by helping them to find new food sources as changes in the weather have an effect on their usual habitats.
